flashcardContentBlock.content: What does a conditional statement guarantee when its condition is met?
It guarantees that another condition must be met as well. The rule leaves no room for exceptions.
What does A → B mean?
If A is true, B must be true. The arrow by itself does not establish a cause or a time order.
“Every order marked ready has been packed.” Does this prove that an order is marked ready?
No. The rule tells us what follows for any order marked ready. It does not tell us that a particular order meets that condition.
“Every order marked ready has been packed.” How do the two groups fit together?
All orders marked ready fit inside the packed-orders group. A ready order cannot sit outside packed. The rule allows packed orders whose ready status is unknown.
Given the rule "All volunteers wear badges" and the fact "Ari is a volunteer," what is guaranteed about Ari?
Ari wears a badge ($\text{Volunteer} \to \text{Wears badge}$). The rule applies to Ari because Ari meets the sufficient condition of being a volunteer.
Why does the direction of a conditional arrow matter?
Switching the arrow changes the claim. A rule guarantees what follows from left to right, not the reverse.
Every order marked ready has been packed. Order B is packed. Do we know whether it is ready?
No. Order B could be marked ready or it could still be waiting for a pickup label. Packed alone does not establish its ready status.
Given "Every volunteer wears a badge," Ari wears a badge. Does this establish Ari is a volunteer?
No. The rule requires volunteers to wear badges, but it does not say only volunteers wear them. Ari could be a staff member wearing a badge.
How are conditional rules used in LSAT Must Be True questions?
You apply a conditional rule to an established fact to draw a guaranteed conclusion that follows the direction of the rule.
What common flaw involves conditional logic on the LSAT?
A flaw occurs when an argument reverses a conditional rule, claiming more than the premises establish by assuming the necessary condition guarantees the sufficient condition.
What is the role of conditional logic in LSAT Sufficient Assumption questions?
You must supply a missing rule that bridges the gap between the given evidence and the conclusion.
Does “Every order marked ready has been packed” require more packed orders than ready orders?
No. All ready orders must be packed, but the rule does not require the groups to differ in size. It allows packed orders outside ready.
What is a sufficient condition?
A condition that is enough to guarantee that another condition occurs. It acts as the trigger for the rule.
On which side of a conditional arrow does the sufficient condition belong?
On the left side ($\text{Sufficient} \to \text{Necessary}$).
If earning full credit is sufficient for passing an assignment, is full credit the only way to pass?
No. Sufficient means enough, not the only way. A student could earn less than full credit and still pass under a different pathway.
Translate "If a person wins the race, that person receives a medal" and identify the sufficient condition.
$\text{Wins} \to \text{Receives medal}$. Winning the race is the sufficient condition because it is enough to guarantee receiving a medal.
What question should you ask yourself to identify if a condition is sufficient?
"If I have this, what must follow?"
What is a necessary condition?
A condition that is required whenever the sufficient condition is met.
On which side of a conditional arrow does the necessary condition belong?
On the right side ($\text{Sufficient} \to \text{Necessary}$).
Does meeting a necessary condition guarantee that the sufficient condition occurs?
No. Necessary means required, not enough. Knowing the necessary condition is met does not trigger the left side.
Translate "Entering the archive requires a pass" and identify the necessary condition.
$\text{Enters archive} \to \text{Has pass}$. Having a pass is necessary because it is required for entry.
Under the rule $\text{Full credit} \to \text{Passes}$, why is passing necessary for earning full credit?
Because you cannot earn full credit and fail. Passing is required whenever full credit is earned.
What question should you ask yourself to identify if a condition is necessary?
"What must I have in order for the left side to be true?"
How do you determine whether a condition is sufficient or necessary?
You read the specific rule in context. Conditions do not have fixed inherent roles; their roles depend on the rule being stated.
What are the seven Group 1 indicators taught in the lesson?
If, when, where, all, the only, every, any.
What side of the arrow does the target of a Group 1 indicator go on?
On the left side. Group 1 indicators introduce the sufficient condition.
What key question must you ask when translating an indicator word?
"What is the indicator referring to?" You must identify the complete target idea.
Translate and explain: "If a student revises the essay, the student receives feedback."
$\text{Revises essay} \to \text{Receives feedback}$. "If" refers to revising the essay, making it the sufficient condition on the left.
Translate and explain: "A student receives feedback if the student revises the essay."
$\text{Revises essay} \to \text{Receives feedback}$. "If" still refers to revising the essay. Sentence word order changed, but the logical relationship did not.
Translate and explain: "When the alarm sounds, the staff evacuate."
$\text{Alarm sounds} \to \text{Staff evacuate}$. "When" refers to the alarm sounding, making it sufficient for staff evacuation.
Translate: “Where a pickup light is green, an order is ready.”
Pickup light is green → Order is ready. “Where” refers to the green pickup light. Under this stated rule, that complete condition goes left.
Translate and explain: "All registered guests receive a wristband."
$\text{Registered guest} \to \text{Receives wristband}$. "All" refers to registered guests, making registration sufficient for getting a wristband.
Translate and explain: "Every volunteer wears a badge."
$\text{Volunteer} \to \text{Wears badge}$. "Every" refers to volunteers, making volunteer status sufficient to guarantee wearing a badge.
Translate and explain: "Any applicant who submits late pays a fee."
$\text{Applicant submits late} \to \text{Pays fee}$. "Any" refers to applicants who submit late, making late submission sufficient for paying a fee.
Why is it incorrect to translate "Any applicant who submits late pays a fee" as $\text{Applicant} \to \text{Pays fee}$?
Because the rule does not apply to all applicants. It only applies to applicants who submit late, so the complete target idea must be kept on the left.
Translate and explain: "The only people admitted are members."
$\text{Admitted} \to \text{Member}$. "The only" refers to people admitted, making being admitted the sufficient condition on the left.
Translate and explain: "A report is reviewed if it is submitted before noon."
$\text{Submitted before noon} \to \text{Reviewed}$. "If" refers to submission before noon, so being submitted before noon guarantees review.
Translate and explain: "The only vehicles permitted inside are electric vehicles."
$\text{Vehicle permitted inside} \to \text{Electric vehicle}$. "The only" refers to vehicles permitted inside, making permission to enter sufficient to establish it is electric.
What are the seven Group 2 indicators taught in the lesson?
Only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must.
What side of the arrow does the target of a Group 2 indicator go on?
On the right side. Group 2 indicators introduce the necessary condition.
Translate and explain: "A student enters the archive only if the student has a pass."
$\text{Enters archive} \to \text{Has pass}$. "Only if" refers to having a pass, making the pass a required (necessary) condition on the right.
Compare the meaning of "A student enters if she has a pass" vs "A student enters only if she has a pass."
"Enters if pass" ($\text{Has pass} \to \text{Enters}$) makes the pass sufficient. "Enters only if pass" ($\text{Enters} \to \text{Has pass}$) makes the pass required.
Translate and explain: "Approval requires a signature."
$\text{Approved} \to \text{Has signature}$. "Requires" points to a signature as the necessary condition on the right.
Translate and explain: "A permit is required for construction."
$\text{Construction} \to \text{Has permit}$. "Required" refers to a permit. The necessary condition appears first in the sentence, but still belongs on the right.
Why must you avoid automatically putting words that physically follow an indicator onto a specific side of the arrow?
Because sentence structure varies. You must ask what complete idea the indicator refers to, identify whether it is sufficient or required, and verify the whole meaning.
Compare "Only members are admitted" and "The only people admitted are members." Do they yield the same rule?
Yes, both translate to $\text{Admitted} \to \text{Member}$. "Only" targets members (required, right). "The only" targets people admitted (sufficient, left).
Translate and explain: "Only registered guests receive wristbands."
$\text{Receives wristband} \to \text{Registered guest}$. "Only" refers to registered guests, making registration required (necessary) on the right.
Translate: “A finalist must attend the interview.” What does the statement establish?
Finalist → Required to attend interview. “Must” states an obligation here. It establishes what finalists are required to do, not that they actually attend.
Translate and explain: "A review occurs only when a complaint is filed."
$\text{Review occurs} \to \text{Complaint filed}$. "Only when" refers to filing a complaint, making the complaint a required condition on the right.
Translate and explain: "The service operates only where a station is available."
$\text{Service operates} \to \text{Station available}$. "Only where" refers to station availability, making it a required condition on the right.
Translate and explain: "A finalist always receives an invitation."
$\text{Finalist} \to \text{Receives invitation}$. "Always" indicates an exceptionless rule requiring that every finalist receives an invitation.
Translate and explain: "A student graduates only if the student completes the project."
$\text{Graduates} \to \text{Completes project}$. "Only if" refers to completing the project, making project completion required on the right.
Contrast how Group 1 indicators differ from Group 2 indicators in conditional translation.
Group 1 indicators (if, when, all, etc.) introduce the sufficient condition (left side). Group 2 indicators (only, required, must, etc.) introduce the necessary condition (right side).
“A finalist must attend the interview.” Maya attended. Does that prove she is a finalist?
No. The rule gives finalists an obligation to attend. It does not say that only finalists attend, or that everyone who attends has that obligation.
“A finalist must attend the interview.” Maya is a finalist. What follows?
Maya is required to attend the interview. We have established her obligation. The statement does not tell us whether she complies.
In the rule $\text{Construction} \to \text{Has permit}$, does having a permit guarantee that construction will happen?
No. Having a permit is required for construction, but possessing a permit does not force someone to build.
Are Group 1 and Group 2 indicators universal mechanical rules?
No. They are teaching guides. You must always read the full sentence context to verify what idea the indicator refers to and check the rule's overall meaning.
What is the difference between sufficient and necessary?
Sufficient means enough to guarantee the other condition. It goes on the left. Necessary means required whenever the sufficient condition is met. It goes on the right.
Why is it a logical flaw to infer $A$ from $B$ given the rule $A \to B$?
Because $B$ is necessary for $A$, not sufficient. $B$ can occur without $A$ occurring.
If full credit guarantees passing ($\text{Full credit} \to \text{Passes}$), why can't we conclude someone earned full credit just because they passed?
Passing is necessary for full credit, but not sufficient. There may be other ways to pass without full credit.
“All volunteers wear badges.” Sam wears a badge. What do we know about his volunteer status?
We cannot determine whether Sam is a volunteer. The rule allows volunteers and other people to wear badges.
“Where a pickup light is green, an order is ready.” An order is ready. Does that establish the pickup light is green?
No. The stated rule makes a green pickup light enough to establish readiness. It does not make readiness enough to establish a green light.
Rule: "When the alarm sounds, the staff evacuate." Fact: "Staff are evacuating." Does this guarantee the alarm sounded?
No ($\text{Alarm sounds} \to \text{Staff evacuate}$). The staff might be evacuating for a scheduled drill without an alarm sounding.
How does adding "only" before "if" change the direction of the arrow?
"If" marks the left side (sufficient). Adding "only" turns it into "only if", which marks the right side (necessary).
Translate "A complaint is filed only when a review occurs."
$\text{Complaint filed} \to \text{Review occurs}$. "Only when" refers to the review occurring, placing it on the right side as a necessary condition.
Translate "The staff evacuate when the alarm sounds."
$\text{Alarm sounds} \to \text{Staff evacuate}$. "When" refers to the alarm sounding, placing it on the left side as a sufficient condition regardless of clause position.
Translate and explain: "Crops grow only where water is abundant."
$\text{Crops grow} \to \text{Water abundant}$. "Only where" refers to abundant water, making it a necessary condition on the right.
Translate and explain: "Where water is abundant, crops grow."
$\text{Water abundant} \to \text{Crops grow}$. "Where" refers to abundant water, making it a sufficient condition on the left.
Translate "Every student who registers early receives a discount."
$\text{Student registers early} \to \text{Receives discount}$. "Every" refers to students who register early, not just any student.
“Reports submitted before noon are reviewed.” A report arrived at 2 PM. Do we know whether it is reviewed?
No. This rule guarantees review for submissions before noon. It leaves later submissions open to being reviewed or not reviewed.
What does “Marked ready → Packed” tell us about an order not marked ready?
This rule does not determine whether that order is packed. An order not marked ready may be packed or unpacked.
Compare "All members are admitted" and "Only members are admitted."

"All members are admitted": $\text{Member} \to \text{Admitted}$ (being a member guarantees admission). "Only members are admitted": $\text{Admitted} \to \text{Member}$ (admission requires being a member).
Translate "A fee is paid by any applicant who submits late."
$\text{Applicant submits late} \to \text{Pays fee}$. "Any" refers to applicants submitting late, placing that complete condition on the left regardless of sentence order.
Translate "Graduation requires completing the project."
$\text{Graduates} \to \text{Completes project}$. "Requires" targets project completion, making it the necessary condition on the right.
Premise 1: $\text{Vehicle permitted inside} \to \text{Electric vehicle}$. Premise 2: Car X is permitted inside. What conclusion MUST be true?
Car X is an electric vehicle. Car X meets the sufficient condition, so the necessary condition guaranteed by the rule must follow.
Premise: $\text{Vehicle permitted inside} \to \text{Electric vehicle}$. Conclusion: Since Car Y is an electric vehicle, Car Y must be permitted inside. What is the logical flaw?
The argument reverses the conditional rule. Being an electric vehicle is required for permission, not sufficient to guarantee entry.
Premise: Ari is a registered guest. Conclusion: Ari receives a wristband. What missing assumption guarantees this conclusion?
$\text{Registered guest} \to \text{Receives wristband}$ ("All registered guests receive a wristband"). This connects the premise fact to the target conclusion.
After translating a sentence into arrow notation, what final step should you take?
Check the meaning of your arrow against the original sentence to ensure the left side genuinely guarantees the right side and the right side is truly required.
Why do "The only A are B" and "Only B are A" produce the same arrow $A \to B$?
Because "The only" points to A as the sufficient condition, while "Only" points to B as the necessary condition. Both express that A cannot exist without B.
